question: What does @Autowired do in Spring?
title: @Autowired Annotation in Spring Explained
direct_answer: **`@Autowired`** tells Spring to automatically inject a dependency. Spring finds a bean of the matching type in the application context and injects it at the annotated field, constructor, or setter. If no matching bean exists, it throws `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core Spring DI injection mechanism knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @Autowired resolves by type first, then by name
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain type-based resolution and the role of @Qualifier when multiple beans exist

sections.title: How @Autowired Resolves
sections.content:
Spring resolves `@Autowired` injection using this process:
1. **By type**: find all beans assignable to the field/parameter type
2. If one match → inject it
3. If multiple matches → use `@Qualifier("name")` or `@Primary` to disambiguate
4. If no match → throw `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` (unless `required=false`)

For interfaces, Spring injects the implementing bean. For `List<SomeBean>`, Spring injects ALL matching beans.

sections.title: @Autowired Usage
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Autowired` is Spring's injection annotation — it tells Spring to find the right bean and inject it here. Spring resolves it primarily by type: if you have `@Autowired UserRepository repo`, Spring looks for a bean of type `UserRepository` in the context and injects it. If there are multiple beans of that type, Spring needs more information — you use `@Qualifier` to specify the exact bean name, or mark one as `@Primary`. If no matching bean exists, Spring throws an exception at startup, unless you set `required=false` to make the injection optional. On constructor injection with a single constructor, `@Autowired` is actually optional since Spring 4.3.

What is the difference between @Autowired and @Inject?

seo.metaTitle: @Autowired in Spring Explained | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn what @Autowired does in Spring, how it resolves by type, and what happens with multiple beans including @Qualifier and @Primary.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: One annotation replaces all the wiring code you'd write by hand — Spring finds the right object and plugs it in for you.

beats.text: @Autowired tells Spring to find a matching bean in the application context and inject it into a field, constructor parameter, or setter. Spring resolves it by type first — it looks for beans whose type matches what you declared. If it finds exactly one, it injects it. If it finds none, it throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup.

Without @Autowired you'd call new on every dependency, creating tight coupling. @Autowired lets Spring own the wiring so your classes don't care how their dependencies are built — they just declare what they need.

items: Field injection: @Autowired directly on the field — convenient but not recommended for production code.
Constructor injection: Spring injects via the constructor — no @Autowired needed if there's a single constructor (Spring 4.3+).
Setter injection: @Autowired on a setter method — useful for optional dependencies with required=false.
Collection injection: @Autowired on List<BeanType> injects all beans of that type at once.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, OrderService depends on UserRepository. You declare private final UserRepository repo in the constructor — Spring sees the single constructor and injects the UserRepository bean automatically. non-obvious: if two beans implement UserRepository, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Add @Qualifier("jpaUserRepository") to tell it which one to use.

items: Don't inject a field marked final with @Autowired — final fields can't be set via reflection. Use constructor injection instead.
Watch out for required=false — the field stays null if no bean exists, which causes NullPointerException at runtime.
Circular dependencies surface as BeanCurrentlyInCreationException — they're usually a design smell, not a Spring bug.

speakable_v2.cap: Think of @Autowired as a declaration, not a command — you're telling Spring what you need, and it figures out how to deliver it.

Why is constructor injection recommended over field injection?

question: What is @Qualifier in Spring and when do you need it?
title: @Qualifier Annotation in Spring
direct_answer: **`@Qualifier("beanName")`** specifies which bean to inject when multiple beans of the same type exist. Without `@Qualifier`, Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. Use it alongside `@Autowired` to select a specific implementation by bean name.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing you can also put @Qualifier on the bean class itself to create a named qualifier
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between @Qualifier and @Primary and when to use each

sections.title: @Qualifier Usage
@Qualifier vs @Primary
sections.content:
- `@Primary`: one bean is the default — used when 90%+ of injections want this implementation
- `@Qualifier`: explicit name-based selection — used when you need a specific non-default bean
- Both can coexist: `@Primary` sets the default, `@Qualifier` overrides per injection point
- `@Qualifier` on the bean class + `@Qualifier` on the injection point must match
- Default qualifier = bean name (class name with lowercase first letter)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Qualifier` is used when you have multiple beans of the same type and need to specify which one to inject. Without it, Spring doesn't know which implementation to choose and throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. You put `@Qualifier("name")` both on the bean class to name it and on the injection point to select it. The difference from `@Primary` is that `@Primary` sets a default — one bean wins when no qualifier is specified. `@Qualifier` is explicit selection regardless of what's primary. The typical pattern is: use `@Primary` on the most common implementation and `@Qualifier` only where you specifically need a different one.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Qualifier and @Primary?
Can you create a custom qualifier annotation?

seo.metaTitle: @Qualifier Spring Annotation | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @Qualifier resolves Spring bean injection ambiguity, the difference from @Primary, and when to use each for multiple implementations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Two beans, same type — Spring panics unless you pick one. @Qualifier is how you make that choice explicit.

beats.text: You're optimising for precise bean selection. When your app has two or more beans implementing the same interface — say StripePaymentService and PayPalPaymentService both implementing PaymentService — Spring can't guess which one to inject. You need a way to name and pick them.

items: @Primary on one bean: marks it as the default. All injection points that don't specify a qualifier get this bean automatically.
@Qualifier on the bean class plus @Qualifier at the injection point: explicit name-based selection. Works regardless of which bean is primary.

Bean name fallback: Spring's default qualifier is the bean's name (class name with lowercase first letter). You can use @Qualifier("stripePaymentService") without putting @Qualifier on the bean class.

values: One impl is used in 90%+ of places
Doesn't help when both are needed in the same class
You need to pinpoint exactly which bean to use
More annotation noise at every injection point

beats.text: candidates miss: the best pattern combines both. Put @Primary on the most commonly used implementation so most injection points need zero extra annotation. Use @Qualifier only at the rare injection points that explicitly need the other bean.

items: You're putting @Qualifier on every single injection point — that's a sign you might not need @Primary or your design has too many generic interfaces.
Your bean names feel arbitrary and hard to remember — consider @Profile to swap implementations per environment instead.

speakable_v2.cap: @Qualifier is a surgical tool — use it sparingly alongside @Primary, not as a replacement for it.

question: What is the difference between @Autowired and @Inject in Spring?
title: @Autowired vs @Inject in Spring
direct_answer: **`@Autowired`** is Spring-specific; **`@Inject`** (from `javax.inject`) is the JSR-330 standard. Both perform the same type-based injection. `@Inject` has no `required` attribute. For Spring applications, `@Autowired` is more common; `@Inject` is used when you want vendor-neutral code.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @Inject exists or thinking they're identical in all aspects

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Autowired` is Spring's own injection annotation while `@Inject` comes from the JSR-330 specification for dependency injection. They both do type-based injection and both work in Spring, but `@Autowired` has Spring-specific features like `required=false`. `@Inject` is useful if you're writing code you want to be portable across DI frameworks — if you ever switch from Spring to Guice, `@Inject` will still work. For Spring-only projects, `@Autowired` is the standard choice. `@Resource` is another option from JSR-250 that resolves by name first rather than type.

followup_questions: What is @Resource and how does it differ from @Autowired?

seo.metaTitle: @Autowired vs @Inject Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Compare Spring @Autowired vs JSR-330 @Inject for dependency injection — similarities, differences, and when to use each in Spring applications.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Both annotations inject beans — the real difference is who wrote the spec and what extra features come along.

groups.heading: @Autowired
groups.text: Spring's own annotation. It resolves by type, then by name. It has a required attribute so you can make a dependency optional with required=false. It's what you'll see in virtually all Spring Boot codebases.

groups.heading: @Inject
groups.text: Comes from the JSR-330 standard (javax.inject package). It also resolves by type and works inside Spring. It doesn't have a required attribute — you'd use Optional<T> instead. It's portable across DI frameworks like Guice.

items: Use @Autowired for all Spring Boot projects — it's idiomatic, well-documented, and supports required=false cleanly.
Use @Inject if you're building a library or framework that should work with multiple DI containers, not just Spring.

beats.text: gotcha: @Resource (JSR-250) is a third option that resolves by name first, then type — the opposite of @Autowired. It's rarely needed but interviewers sometimes ask about it. In our Spring Boot app, stick with @Autowired unless you have a specific portability requirement.

speakable_v2.cap: @Autowired is the Spring-native choice; @Inject buys portability at the cost of one feature. For most freshers, @Autowired is all you need to know cold.
followup_handoff: What is @Resource and how does its resolution order differ from @Autowired?
When would a library author prefer @Inject over @Autowired?

question: What happens if Spring cannot find a bean for @Autowired injection?
title: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException in Spring
direct_answer: Spring throws **`NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`** at startup if a required `@Autowired` dependency has no matching bean. This is a fail-fast behavior — the application won't start until all required dependencies are satisfied. Use `@Autowired(required=false)` for optional injection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Debugging knowledge for common Spring startup issues
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not understanding why the error happens — usually a missing @Component or wrong package
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: List the common causes: missing annotation, wrong package, wrong type, no bean registered

sections.title: Common Causes of NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
sections.content:
1. **Missing stereotype annotation**: forgot `@Service` or `@Repository` on the class
2. **Package outside scan range**: class is in a package Spring doesn't scan
3. **Wrong type**: `@Autowired UserService service` but only `UserServiceImpl` bean exists (won't match if it doesn't implement `UserService`)
4. **Conditional bean disabled**: `@ConditionalOnProperty` condition not met
5. **Profile not active**: `@Profile("prod")` bean but profile is `dev`
6. **Missing dependency**: `@Bean` method not in a `@Configuration` class that gets scanned

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Thrown at **startup** — fail-fast (good for catching config errors early)
- `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type ...`
- Debugging steps: check annotation, check package, enable debug mode
- `@Autowired(required=false)` suppresses exception for optional deps
- `Optional<BeanType>` also allows nullable injection without exception
- Use `@SpringBootTest` + `@Autowired` to verify beans in tests

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When Spring can't find a bean for an `@Autowired` field, it throws `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup — the app won't start. This fail-fast behavior is actually helpful because you find configuration problems immediately. The most common causes are: forgetting to add `@Service` or `@Component` on the class, putting the class in a package that's outside the component scan range, or a type mismatch where the field expects an interface but no bean implements it. To debug, enable `debug=true` in application.properties to see the conditions evaluation report. If the dependency is optional, use `@Autowired(required=false)` and the field stays null if no matching bean exists.

seo.metaTitle: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn what causes NoSuchBeanDefinitionException in Spring, why it's thrown at startup, and how to debug and fix missing bean injection errors.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Your app won't start, the error mentions 'No qualifying bean' — this is Spring's way of failing loudly rather than failing silently later.

beats.text: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException is thrown at startup when Spring tries to inject a required @Autowired dependency but can't find any bean that matches the declared type. It's a fail-fast check — the application context won't finish loading until every required dependency is resolved. This catches configuration bugs immediately instead of at runtime.

Spring's fail-fast startup means you'd rather crash loudly in 5 seconds than discover a null reference three hours into production. This exception is Spring protecting you from runtime NullPointerExceptions that are much harder to diagnose.

items: Missing stereotype annotation: the class exists but doesn't have @Service, @Component, or @Repository, so Spring never registers it as a bean.
Wrong package: the class is outside the component scan base package, so Spring never finds it during scanning.
Type mismatch: the field expects UserService (an interface) but the registered bean is UserServiceImpl without implementing it.
Disabled by condition: @ConditionalOnProperty or @Profile means the bean isn't created in the current environment.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, if OrderService @Autowires UserRepository but you forgot @Repository on UserRepository, Spring throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type 'UserRepository'. production trap: add debug=true to application.properties — Spring prints the full conditions evaluation report showing exactly why each bean was or wasn't created. That log is your fastest debugging tool.

items: Don't silence the error with required=false unless the dependency is truly optional — a null field is just a delayed crash.
Check that @SpringBootApplication is in the parent package of all your @Service and @Repository classes — it defines the scan boundary.

speakable_v2.cap: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException is a configuration bug, not a Spring bug — the fix is almost always a missing annotation or a package outside the scan range.

question: How does @Autowired work with collections?
title: @Autowired with Collections in Spring
direct_answer: When `@Autowired` is on a `List<BeanType>` or `Map<String, BeanType>`, Spring **injects all beans** of that type into the collection. This is useful for plugin-style architectures where you process all registered beans of a type.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing this is possible — trying to inject all implementations manually
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real example: Strategy pattern with a list of handlers

sections.title: Injecting All Implementations
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Autowired List<BeanType>` → all beans of that type injected
- `@Autowired Map<String, BeanType>` → bean name → bean instance mapping
- Order: use `@Order(1)` or implement `Ordered` to control list order
- `@Autowired Set<BeanType>` also works
- Common pattern: **Strategy pattern** — select handler based on runtime condition
- Good for plugin-style architectures: add new implementations without modifying the orchestrator

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You can `@Autowired` a `List<SomeInterface>` and Spring will inject all beans that implement that interface. This is really powerful for the Strategy pattern or plugin architectures. For example, if you have multiple payment handlers — Stripe, PayPal, bank transfer — each implementing a `PaymentHandler` interface, you can inject them all as a list and then at runtime pick the right one based on the payment type. Adding a new payment method is just adding a new `@Component` class — you don't touch the `PaymentService` at all. You can also inject them as a `Map<String, BeanType>` where the keys are bean names.

followup_questions: How do you control the order of beans in an @Autowired list?
What is the Strategy design pattern?
How does Map<String, Bean> injection work?

seo.metaTitle: @Autowired with Collections Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @Autowired works with List and Map collections in Spring to inject all implementations of an interface for Strategy pattern implementations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Declare one List field and Spring silently rounds up every matching bean in the context — you never have to manually register handlers again.

beats.text: When @Autowired targets a List<SomeInterface>, Spring injects every bean in the context that implements that interface into the list. It's the same resolution logic as single-bean injection, except Spring doesn't stop at the first match — it collects them all. You can also use Map<String, BeanType> to get a map from bean name to bean instance.

It's the backbone of the Strategy and Plugin patterns. Instead of hard-coding each handler in your orchestrator, you let Spring discover them. Adding a new implementation is just adding a new @Component class — the orchestrator doesn't change at all.

items: List injection: Spring injects all beans of the declared element type, in undefined order by default.
Ordered list: add @Order(1), @Order(2) on your beans to control their position in the injected list.
Map injection: Map<String, BeanType> gives you bean name as key and bean instance as value — useful for lookup by string key.
Set injection: Set<BeanType> also works if you don't care about order or duplicates.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, PaymentService declares private List<PaymentHandler> handlers. StripeHandler and PayPalHandler both implement PaymentHandler and carry @Component. At startup Spring injects both into the list. At runtime, PaymentService calls handlers.stream().filter(h -> h.supports(type)).findFirst(). sharp edge: to add a new payment method later, just create a third @Component class — zero changes to PaymentService. That's the open-closed principle in action.

items: Don't assume list order — it's not deterministic without @Order or implementing the Ordered interface.
If the list is empty at runtime, no beans matched the type. Check your component scan and that each handler carries @Component.

speakable_v2.cap: Collection injection turns @Autowired into a discovery mechanism — let Spring assemble the list so your code stays open to extension.
followup_handoff: How does @Order control the position of beans in an injected List?
How does Map<String, BeanType> injection differ from List injection?

question: What is @Primary in Spring and when do you use it?
title: @Primary Annotation in Spring
direct_answer: **`@Primary`** marks one bean as the default candidate when multiple beans of the same type exist. Spring uses it when no `@Qualifier` is specified. Use `@Primary` on the most commonly used implementation so you only need `@Qualifier` at the rare injection points that need the alternative.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Qualifier everywhere instead of @Primary for the common case

sections.title: @Primary Usage
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Primary`: marks the default bean when there are multiple candidates
- Without `@Qualifier`, Spring uses the `@Primary` bean
- `@Qualifier` overrides `@Primary` — more specific wins
- Only one bean per type should be `@Primary`
- Also usable on `@Bean` factory methods
- If multiple beans are `@Primary` → still ambiguous → `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Primary` is used when you have multiple beans of the same type and want to designate one as the default without annotating every injection point. If you have two `CacheService` implementations and most of your code should use Redis, you put `@Primary` on the `RedisCacheService`. Now all `@Autowired CacheService` injections get Redis automatically. Only the rare places that specifically need the in-memory cache need to use `@Qualifier`. This is the cleanest pattern: `@Primary` for the common case, `@Qualifier` for explicit overrides. The rule is: at most one `@Primary` per type.

followup_questions: Can you have multiple @Primary beans of the same type?

seo.metaTitle: @Primary Spring Annotation | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how @Primary designates a default Spring bean for type-based injection, how it works with @Qualifier, and the @Primary + @Qualifier pattern.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Primary is the 'silent default' — most injection points get the right bean with zero extra annotation.

beats.text: @Primary marks one bean as the preferred candidate when Spring finds multiple beans of the same type. When you inject by type and don't specify @Qualifier, Spring picks the @Primary bean. It's a way to say 'in case of ambiguity, choose this one' at the bean definition level rather than at every injection point.

Without @Primary, having two beans of the same type always forces you to add @Qualifier to every injection point. That's repetitive. @Primary lets you declare the default once and only use @Qualifier for the exceptions.

items: On a @Service or @Component class: that class becomes the default bean for its type across the whole context.
On a @Bean method inside @Configuration: the returned bean becomes primary for its return type.
Combined with @Qualifier: @Qualifier always wins. @Primary is only consulted when no qualifier is present.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, RedisCacheService and InMemoryCacheService both implement CacheService. Ninety percent of services want Redis, so you put @Primary on RedisCacheService. Now every @Autowired CacheService field gets Redis automatically. The one integration test that needs the in-memory version uses @Qualifier("inMemoryCacheService"). non-obvious: if you mark both as @Primary, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException — you're back to square one.

items: Never mark two beans of the same type as @Primary — it doesn't break the tie, it just throws a different exception.
Don't use @Primary as a workaround for a design that needs proper @Qualifier — if you need different beans in many places, use @Qualifier explicitly.

speakable_v2.cap: Use @Primary to set a sensible default and @Qualifier to override it precisely — together they eliminate annotation noise across your codebase.
